# TaskerArmy Slack notification component

This component turns an actionable job revision into a concise Slack notice with a link to its current review page. It includes authenticated event receiving, a persistent delivery queue, tenant/store/channel routing, saved delivery outcomes and operator recovery commands. It runs with Python 3.11 or later and SQLite from the standard library.

The integration follows TaskerArmy's [planned Slack workflow](https://taskerarmy.com/integrations/slack/): notify the people who need to act, then return them to the product to review the job. The source event envelope below belongs to this component. TaskerArmy's existing job publisher maps its actual internal events into that envelope.

## What the merchant receives

Each notice contains the job title, store identifier, actionable state, a short reason, the job revision and an authenticated review link. Titles and reasons render as plain text. The review link uses a standard Slack link, so the webhook installation needs no interactive-button callback.

|Event state|Notice|Review action|
|---|---|---|
|clarification_required|Clarification required|Provide clarification|
|execution_blocked|Execution needs attention|Review the next step|
|qa_failed|QA needs attention|Review the failed check|
|preview_ready|Preview ready|Review the preview|
|approval_requested|Approval requested|Review in the dashboard|
|quiet|Retires queued notices for an older job revision|Current job state stays in the product|

A route selects the tenant, one or more stores, allowed event states and an installed Slack channel. One event produces at most one notice per matching workspace/channel, even when multiple rules match. Newer job revisions supersede older queued notices. A request already in flight can finish; every notice retains its revision and points to the current product review.

## Install and initialize

Save `notification_outbox.py` and this guide together. Use an ordinary persistent directory on the application host.

```sh
python --version
python notification_outbox.py --config notices.json --db state/notices.sqlite3 init
```

The initialization command creates an empty private configuration and database. It refuses to overwrite an existing configuration. The program uses no package installation, cloud queue or recurring third-party service.

Deploy the receiver and worker against the same local SQLite database. SQLite WAL and an immediate write transaction coordinate multiple processes on that host. Keep the database on local persistent storage and use the application's existing process supervisor.

### Configure an actual Slack installation

In the customer's Slack app, enable Incoming Webhooks and install the webhook into the intended channel. Record the workspace ID and channel ID returned by that installation. Put its secret URL in the application's secret environment as `TASKER_SLACK_WEBHOOK`. Put a separate random ingress token of at least 32 characters in `TASKER_INGRESS_TOKEN`.

The service's environment also needs these ordinary values while creating the configuration:

|Environment value|Value from the actual installation|
|---|---|
|TASKER_TENANT_ID|Product tenant identifier|
|TASKER_STORE_ID|Product store identifier|
|TASKER_SLACK_TEAM_ID|Installed Slack workspace ID|
|TASKER_SLACK_CHANNEL_ID|Installed Slack channel ID|
|TASKER_REVIEW_ORIGIN|Canonical HTTPS dashboard origin, such as the product's current https://dashboard.taskerarmy.com origin|

Use those actual values to fill the initialized configuration:

```sh
python - <<'PY'
import json
import os
from pathlib import Path

tenant = os.environ["TASKER_TENANT_ID"]
config = {
    "version": 1,
    "product_name": "TaskerArmy",
    "tenants": {
        tenant: {
            "ingress_token_env": "TASKER_INGRESS_TOKEN",
            "review_origins": [os.environ["TASKER_REVIEW_ORIGIN"]],
        }
    },
    "routes": [{
        "id": "merchant-review",
        "tenant_id": tenant,
        "store_ids": [os.environ["TASKER_STORE_ID"]],
        "states": [
            "clarification_required", "execution_blocked", "qa_failed",
            "preview_ready", "approval_requested",
        ],
        "team_id": os.environ["TASKER_SLACK_TEAM_ID"],
        "channel_id": os.environ["TASKER_SLACK_CHANNEL_ID"],
        "webhook_env": "TASKER_SLACK_WEBHOOK",
        "generation": 1,
        "enabled": True,
    }],
}
Path("notices.json").write_text(json.dumps(config, indent=2) + "\n", encoding="utf-8")
PY
python notification_outbox.py status
```

A webhook is bound to the channel selected during installation. The route's IDs describe that actual installation; changing an event cannot change its destination. Use another installed webhook and route for a different channel. Multiple tenants use separate ingress-token environment references and server-owned routes. Use `store_ids: ["*"]` only when that tenant has chosen to receive notices for all its stores.

The configuration stores environment references, not webhook secrets. Its review origins are exact HTTPS origins without trailing slashes. Event review URLs must use one of those origins and contain the actual authenticated job path. The URL accepts no credentials, query or fragment. The source application supplies the real path from its router.

## Connect the job publisher

The source application emits one normalized envelope for each relevant job revision. It authenticates the tenant from its existing job context and retains the event in its existing durable event publisher until the receiving operation is acknowledged.

|Field|Source meaning|
|---|---|
|event_id|Stable event ID, reused unchanged when the same event is retried|
|job_id|Actual stable job ID|
|store_id|Actual store belonging to the authenticated tenant and job|
|version|Positive, monotonically increasing job revision|
|state|One of the six states listed above|
|title|Customer-safe job title, at most 180 characters|
|reason|Optional short explanation, at most 500 characters|
|review_url|Actual HTTPS job-review URL on a configured tenant origin|
|occurred_at|Source event time in ISO 8601 with a timezone|

Do not include a tenant, webhook, Slack channel, source code or credentials inside the envelope. Tenant identity comes from the authenticated receiving header or the trusted local caller. State changes that make an older notice irrelevant should emit a newer `quiet` revision. Replaying an old event does not create a new notice.

### Option A: authenticated HTTP receiving

Run the receiver:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port 8094
```

The source publisher sends `POST /v1/events` with JSON, a correct Content-Length, `X-Notification-Tenant` set to its authorized tenant, and `Authorization: Bearer` followed by that tenant's ingress secret. Receiving allows bodies up to 32,768 bytes. Keep the listener on loopback; a separate host uses the application's existing HTTPS ingress and network controls.

An HTTP 202 response means the envelope was durably classified and committed. The body identifies `recorded`, `duplicate`, `stale` or `expired`, together with the number of queued notices. The source publisher can acknowledge that event for all four outcomes. An invalid envelope receives 400; fix its source mapping. An unavailable receiver responds 503. If the publisher loses its HTTP response, it retries the exact same event ID and content.

The source job transaction and this component's SQLite transaction are separate. The source application's durable event publisher is what preserves a job transition across that boundary; enqueue the event with the job change or use the application's existing transactional event mechanism.

### Option B: same-host Python caller

Import the component in the product's existing durable event consumer:

```python
from notification_outbox import Outbox

notices = Outbox("state/notices.sqlite3", "notices.json")
result = notices.record(authenticated_tenant_id, normalized_job_event)
```

Both arguments come from that consumer's actual job event and authorized tenant context. The return value has the same classification as HTTP receiving. Reuse a stable source event ID across consumer retries.

### Operate a retained actual event

Save a normalized actual event as `job-event.json`, then inspect its message and receive it:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py render --tenant "$TASKER_TENANT_ID" --event job-event.json
python notification_outbox.py ingest --tenant "$TASKER_TENANT_ID" --event job-event.json
python notification_outbox.py status --tenant "$TASKER_TENANT_ID"
```

The render command prepares the message without sending it. The ingest command commits the event and its immutable message to SQLite. Repeating the ingest command with the same bytes resolves as a duplicate and queues zero additional messages. Reusing the ID for different content returns an error.

## Run delivery

Start the persistent worker with the same configuration, database and secret environment:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py run
```

For a supervised one-pass operation:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py deliver --limit 100
python notification_outbox.py status
```

The worker posts the exact message saved at ingest time and retains its SHA-256, event, route fingerprint, workspace/channel, attempt count and outcome. It reserves each destination for at least 1.1 seconds between posts. Slack HTTP 429 responses defer that channel until Retry-After has elapsed. Work for other channels can continue.

A normal successful incoming-webhook response is HTTP 200 with the plain body `ok`. The queue records that acknowledgement and time. The webhook response does not contain a Slack message timestamp. When support needs the message link, retrieve it from the actual channel history or the installation's Events API receiving.

The complete message is retrievable with:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py inspect "$TASKER_DELIVERY_ID"
```

This command includes the actual retained event, message, destination and delivery outcome. Its output is suitable for the customer's own operating record; it contains the short job summary and review URL.

Read the complete job history in pages, including quiet revisions and each revision's receiving outcomes:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py timeline --tenant "$TASKER_TENANT_ID" --job "$TASKER_JOB_ID"
```

When `next_before_version` is present, pass that value as `--before-version` on the following call. The history preserves every recorded revision.

## Recover an interrupted operation

The worker commits a dispatch lease before transmitting. A post that loses its response becomes `uncertain`. If the process stops while a request is active, an expired dispatch lease becomes `uncertain` on the next worker pass. Such a message stays available for reconciliation, preserving its exact body and destination.

Inspect the actual channel at the retained attempt time. When the message exists, record its actual link in the resolution note:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py resolve "$TASKER_DELIVERY_ID" sent --note "$TASKER_ACTUAL_MESSAGE_LINK"
```

When the receiving history establishes that replay is appropriate, use:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py resolve "$TASKER_DELIVERY_ID" retry --note "$TASKER_REPLAY_REASON"
python notification_outbox.py deliver
```

A deliberate cancellation uses `cancelled` with a short reason. Slack incoming webhooks cannot retract messages already posted; the product review remains the current source of job state.

|Saved state|Meaning and operating action|
|---|---|
|pending|Queued or waiting for channel timing; the worker continues it|
|dispatching|One worker currently owns the transmit lease|
|sent|Slack acknowledged the post, or an operator reconciled its actual receiving|
|uncertain|Transmitted operation needs receiving reconciliation before replay|
|route_failed|Slack rejected a route or payload; repair its installation or content|
|route_changed|The original route changed; retain it for explicit reconciliation|
|failed|A delivery needs operator repair after a terminal response or exhausted server retries|
|superseded|A newer job revision retired this queued notice|
|expired|The notice exceeded its event lifetime|
|cancelled|An operator ended this delivery with a recorded reason|

HTTP 5xx responses use a capped exponential retry schedule; eight failed server attempts require operator repair. A definitive invalid-payload, archived-channel, prohibited-action or invalid-installation response stops that route until it is corrected. Pending notices for that route remain saved while the other routes continue.

After restoring the same channel's webhook secret or correcting its installation, resume it:

```sh
python notification_outbox.py resume-route merchant-review
```

When a route changes tenant, store selection, channel, event selection or installation identity, update its configuration and increment `generation`. Older queued notices keep their original destination fingerprint. A new destination receives a new product revision through the normal event publisher.

Default event lifetime is 24 hours from the source event time. A local consumer can pass `ttl_seconds` between 60 and 604800 to `record`. Replayed expired events still advance the recorded job revision, preventing an older queued message from becoming current again.

## Operating console

The complete package includes the local operator console, with tenant/channel setup, route and event preferences, a delivery queue, explicit recovery and paginated job history. Start it alongside the existing receiver and worker:

~~~sh
python operator_server.py --database state/notices.sqlite3 --config notices.json --port 8095
~~~

Open the local link printed by the process. The console uses the same saved outbox and the same live configuration. Its separate operator token authorizes local administration; each tenant retains its own ingress credential. Follow [the complete operator guide](OPERATOR.md) for first setup, configuration changes and daily recovery.

## Operate and hand over

The deployed service consists of the complete Python source, this guide, the customer's private configuration, the SQLite database and the launching environment. Back up SQLite using its native backup API or the host's consistent database snapshot procedure. Preserve the configuration beside that backup and restore secrets through the customer's existing secret service.

The status output supplies delivery counts, recent outcomes and failed route summaries. Use the existing application monitor to surface `uncertain`, `route_failed`, `route_changed` and terminal `failed` counts. Keep job detail in TaskerArmy; Slack receives the short actionable summary.

A completed installation follows an actual job revision from its durable publisher into this queue, shows the selected notice in the installed Slack channel, follows its real review link, and reopens the saved receiving record after a worker restart. A second ingestion of the same source event leaves the message count unchanged. This operating sequence is the handover result.

# Operate TaskerArmy notification delivery

The operator console works on the same durable outbox and routing configuration as `notification_outbox.py`. It supplies complete tenant and Slack-route setup, a current delivery queue, explicit recovery and the original job's retained event history.

`operator_server.py` imports the maintained `Outbox` and `load_config` directly. `operator.html` is its self-contained browser interface. Python 3.11+ and the standard library are sufficient on the existing Linux host. The console uses the worker's own SQLite methods; each method opens and closes its connection.

## Start on the existing worker host

First follow the main README to initialize the database/configuration and start the ingress and delivery worker. Pass the **same absolute database and configuration paths** to the console:

```sh
python operator_server.py \
  --database /absolute/path/to/state/notices.sqlite3 \
  --config /absolute/path/to/notices.json \
  --port 8095
```

Open the local URL printed by this command. The server binds to `127.0.0.1`. The generated operator token is carried in the URL fragment, read into browser memory, and immediately removed from the address bar. It is sent to local API routes only through the Authorization header. The page does not save it in browser storage.

The process creates a new random token on each launch. An operator can supply an existing URL-safe token of at least 32 characters in `TASKER_OPERATOR_TOKEN`, or name a different environment variable with `--token-env`. Keep that token with the host's existing administrative credentials. The tenant's ingress token has a separate receiving purpose.

For a remote host, use an existing SSH connection and a local port forward. Keep the browser's forwarded address at the same loopback port as the server:

```sh
ssh -N -L 8095:127.0.0.1:8095 user@existing-host
```

Open `http://127.0.0.1:8095/` and enter the operator token from that process. Host and Origin checks expect that exact local address. The console is a host operator interface. A future embedding in TaskerArmy's authenticated product must resolve its own administrative role and tenant membership before exposing the same methods.

## Set up the first tenant and route

An empty initialized configuration is supported. Open **Connections & routing**, then:

1. **Add tenant.** Use the original tenant identity that the product's authenticated job transition resolves. Enter the allowed HTTPS review origin and the name of the host environment variable holding this tenant's ingress credential.
2. **Install the Slack incoming webhook** through the current Slack application/installation workflow. Save its credential in the delivery worker's host environment.
3. **Add route.** Record the actual Slack team and channel returned by that installation, the webhook environment-variable name, the tenant and the desired stores. `*` covers every store in that tenant.
4. Choose the actionable events that the team wants: clarification required, execution blocked, QA failed, preview ready or approval requested. New routes initially select preview ready.
5. Save. The existing delivery worker reads the updated configuration on its next operation.

A Slack incoming webhook has a fixed installed destination. Recording another channel ID in this console does not change the webhook's destination. Install/configure the correct destination first, then record its actual metadata and credential reference.

The UI shows whether referenced credentials exist in **the operator process's environment**. When ingress, worker and operator are separate services, configure each service with the credentials it actually uses. A missing operator environment variable does not by itself describe another process's environment.

The console stores variable names, approved origins and routing metadata. Actual receiving tokens and webhook URLs stay in the host's existing environment/secret management.

## Change routing while work continues

Each configuration read returns the SHA-256 of its exact complete source document. Saving compares that revision under a local writer lock, validates the complete replacement with the maintained worker loader, writes a private temporary file and atomically replaces the original configuration.

If another operator changed the source, the save returns `configuration_changed`. The form stays open with the unsaved values so the operator can compose the change against the current configuration.

A material route edit changes its generation: tenant, store selection, event selection, installed Slack team/channel or webhook-variable reference. The console increments the generation automatically. Enable/disable remains an explicit route setting. A saved route generation cannot decrease. The original worker's routing fingerprint keeps already queued notifications attached to their original destination and routing generation.

The worker also checks each queued notification's original review link against the tenant's current approved origins before dispatch. Revoking an origin retains the queued notice as `route_changed` with `review_origin_changed`; its original event and message remain available for the operator.

Use this console/API or the same `.operator.lock` when multiple configuration writers operate on the host. Atomic replacement gives worker readers a complete document. The current JSON file is retained as the operator's actual configuration; no product deployment or worker restart is needed for its ordinary reloading behavior.

## Operate the delivery queue

The queue reads the newest 200 saved deliveries for the chosen tenant, with counts calculated by the maintained outbox. Filter this receiving window by state, job or route. **Export visible CSV** exports precisely the displayed rows and protects spreadsheet text fields against formula interpretation.

The four summary values are:

| View | Included worker states |
| --- | --- |
| Waiting | `pending`, `dispatching` |
| Delivered | `sent`, including operator-confirmed receiving |
| Needs attention | `uncertain`, `route_failed`, `route_changed`, `failed` |
| Retained history | `superseded`, `expired`, `cancelled` |

Open **Inspect** to see the original event identity/version, route, destination, immutable message digest, attempt count, timing, last response and saved resolution. Where the original event is present, the console renders its concise notification and approved review link.

**Connections need attention** shows the worker's recorded route failures. Repair the original Slack connection, then choose **Resume connection**. This calls `resume_route`; it resumes only failed rows matching the currently enabled route's fingerprint.

### Resolve a saved delivery

The worker permits operator resolution for `uncertain`, `failed`, `route_changed` and `route_failed`. The console uses the original `resolve` method and records an operator note with the decision.

- **Received in Slack — mark sent:** record that the original notification was received.
- **Retry the original notification:** return the retained original message to the worker's ordinary dispatch path.
- **Cancel this notification:** retain the event and close its delivery.

Before retrying an uncertain response, inspect the installed Slack channel. A transport failure may have occurred after Slack accepted the message. The original event/message remains the recovery reference.

Retry requires the unchanged route fingerprint. The worker's claim step still applies expiry, newer job versions and current route availability. A resolution does not manufacture a new event or skip those checks.

The console does not start another delivery loop. The existing worker remains responsible for dispatch, leases, provider responses and due times.

## Reopen a complete job history

Choose **Job history**, select its original tenant and enter the job ID. Clicking a job in the delivery table opens the same view.

The console calls `job_timeline(tenant_id, job_id, before_version, limit)`. Numeric delivery identities and job revisions travel as exact decimal strings in the browser API, preserving SQLite revision cursors beyond JavaScript's integer range. It shows the current job head, retained events including quiet/stale revisions, and each original delivery's status, attempts and resolution. **Load earlier revisions** follows the returned `next_before_version`; it does not assume the recent-delivery window contains the entire job.

A source notification opens the authenticated TaskerArmy review page. Merchant approval and publishing continue in that product workflow.

## Local API

Every `/api/` request uses the current operator Bearer token. All mutation routes are POST and expect JSON.

| Method and path | Actual maintained behavior |
| --- | --- |
| `GET /api/config` | Return validated configuration, exact source revision and environment-reference availability |
| `POST /api/config` | Compare `expected_revision`, validate and atomically replace `configuration` |
| `GET /api/status?tenant_id=…&limit=200` | Call `Outbox.status`; an omitted tenant reads this operator's configured tenants |
| `GET /api/deliveries/{id}` | Call `inspect` and return the saved public delivery fields |
| `GET /api/jobs?tenant_id=…&job_id=…&before_version=…&limit=50` | Call the paginated original job timeline |
| `POST /api/resume-route` | Call `resume_route` for `route_id` |
| `POST /api/resolve` | Call `resolve` for `delivery_id`, `resolution` and `note` |
| `GET /healthz` | Local operator process health |

This is the package's local operator API. TaskerArmy's private production API is integrated through the original authenticated job-transition hook described in the main README.

## Operating controls

The server accepts only its printed loopback Host and a matching browser Origin. Browser API calls use a separate random administrative token. Requests have explicit content types and body limits. Saved configuration carries only supported fields and rejects unexpected fields.

The browser uses a content-security policy with hashes of its actual script and stylesheet, has no external assets, renders event text through DOM text nodes, and strips the launch fragment. Access logs exclude request URLs and authorization material. The server projects delivery fields instead of returning private dispatch leases.

Automatic refresh runs every 15 seconds while the authenticated tab is visible. It pauses while a form/detail dialog is open, stops after authentication failure, and coalesces overlapping refreshes. Close the console process with Ctrl-C when finished; the existing ingress and worker processes continue independently.

## Receiving the complete implementation

Run the completed worker and console together on the original equipped Linux host. Exercise an empty configuration through tenant/route setup, record the five documented job states through the actual ingress/callable boundary, inspect the retained deliveries and job timeline, and reopen after restarting the console. Use the existing controlled transport receiving to exercise provider delay, revocation and uncertain-response resolution before the owner's real installed channel commissioning.

Verify the browser at desktop and phone width, including a real configuration conflict and the recovery form. The module does not introduce dependencies, CI jobs or a separate generated test catalogue. Actual run results and the complete installed source belong in the original TaskerArmy case.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Start the original operator on an installed notification workspace."""
from __future__ import annotations
import argparse, importlib.util, json, os, pathlib, re, secrets, sys, uuid
sys.dont_write_bytecode = True
import manage
import archive as package

def main(argv=None):
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--directory", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--ready-file", required=True)
    parser.add_argument("--port", type=int, default=0)
    parser.add_argument("--token-env", default="TASKER_OPERATOR_TOKEN")
    args = parser.parse_args(argv)
    if not 0 <= args.port <= 65535:
        parser.error("port must be between 0 and 65535")
    current = manage.installation(args.directory)
    application = pathlib.Path(current["paths"]["application"])
    source = manage.ordinary(application / "operator_server.py")
    html = manage.ordinary(application / "operator.html")
    # These two original modules are selected from the same installed source.
    worker = manage.worker_module(application)
    sys.modules["notification_outbox"] = worker
    spec = importlib.util.spec_from_file_location("taskerarmy_original_operator", source)
    operator = importlib.util.module_from_spec(spec)
    spec.loader.exec_module(operator)
    token = os.environ.get(args.token_env) or secrets.token_urlsafe(48)
    if len(token) < 32 or not re.fullmatch(r"[A-Za-z0-9_-]+", token):
        raise ValueError("The selected operator credential must be at least 32 URL-safe characters")
    ready = pathlib.Path(args.ready_file).absolute()
    if ready.exists() or ready.is_symlink():
        raise FileExistsError("Use a new ready file for this exact process")
    server = operator.OperatorServer(args.port, pathlib.Path(current["paths"]["database"]),
        pathlib.Path(current["paths"]["configuration"]), token, html.read_bytes())
    identity = {"schema": "taskerarmy.operator-process.v1", "instance_id": str(uuid.uuid4()),
        "installation_id": current["installation_id"], "operation_id": current["operation_id"],
        "pid": os.getpid(), "started_at": manage.utc(), "origin": server.origin,
        "url": server.origin + "/#token=" + token, "application": str(application),
        "database": current["paths"]["database"], "configuration": current["paths"]["configuration"],
        "operator_source_sha256": package.digest_file(source), "html_sha256": package.digest_file(html)}
    package.atomic_json(ready, identity)
    print(json.dumps({key: value for key, value in identity.items() if key != "url"}), flush=True)
    try:
        server.serve_forever(poll_interval=0.25)
    except KeyboardInterrupt:
        pass
    finally:
        server.server_close()
    return 0

if __name__ == "__main__":
    try:
        raise SystemExit(main())
    except (ValueError, OSError) as exc:
        print(json.dumps({"error": type(exc).__name__, "detail": str(exc)}), file=sys.stderr, flush=True)
        raise SystemExit(2)

# Installed TaskerArmy notification workspace

This directory supplies the native installation and JSON operation interface for the complete TaskerArmy notification application. The installed worker, operator console, routing configuration and SQLite history form one application. The source selection, editable installed application and original source baseline remain available through a complete handover.

The worker's event contract, route selection, channel pacing and delivery recovery are described in [the application guide](../README.md). Tenant and connection setup, delivery inspection and job history are described in [the operator guide](../OPERATOR.md). The complete machine interface is in [API.md](API.md).

## Prepare an installation

Use Python 3.11 or later on a Linux or another POSIX host with SQLite and file locks. The application uses the Python standard library. Choose an ordinary, complete product source directory, a private routing configuration file, and a separate new private installation directory.

The supplied configuration.empty.json is an actual empty configuration accepted by the original loader. Copy it to the intended private configuration path, then configure tenants and routes through the operator or configuration.save. It contains no connection credentials.

From the selected product source:

~~~sh
python3 -B native/manage.py prepare \
  --application /SELECTED/products/taskerarmy \
  --configuration /PRIVATE/notices.json \
  --directory /PRIVATE/taskerarmy-installation \
  --operation-id YOUR-RETAINED-INSTALLATION-ID
~~~

The original preparer copies every selected source file into the original source baseline and the editable application, captures the selected configuration, initializes the original SQLite tables, and records the interpreter and directory identity. Retain the exact operation ID and source selection. Repeating that same completed selection returns its original installation.

The installation record contains its UUID, operation ID, complete source-manifest identity, selected Python executable and version, and absolute application/configuration/database paths. Directory binding includes the actual canonical path, device and inode. An installation should be received through the archive operation when moving to another directory or host.

Read the complete installed source and database inventory with:

~~~sh
python3 -B native/manage.py inspect --directory /PRIVATE/taskerarmy-installation
~~~

Inspect verifies the complete original source baseline and all original database tables. The application remains editable, while its original baseline is retained separately.

## Use the installed JSON operations

The stable entrypoint accepts one UTF-8 JSON request through stdin or an explicitly selected file:

~~~sh
python3 -B native/operations.py --request /PRIVATE/operation.json
~~~

A request has the taskerarmy.operation-request.v1 schema, a declared operation, its arguments, and the selected installation when applicable. Configuration writes, event receiving and recovery mutations require a retained request_id. The success or error response is one JSON document; the process exits 0 or 2.

For example, a saved installation can be inspected without starting any services:

~~~json
{
  "schema": "taskerarmy.operation-request.v1",
  "operation": "installation.inspect",
  "installation": "/PRIVATE/taskerarmy-installation",
  "arguments": {}
}
~~~

Use installation.prepare and installation.receive for initial materialization. All installed operations load native/manage.py, native/archive.py, notification_outbox.py and operator_server.py from that installation's selected application. The original installation lock spans source selection and the operation. Original lifecycle methods reuse that held lock; the operator and worker retain their original configuration and SQLite concurrency.

The shared application supervisor can call commands.describe and run the returned executable, argument array and working directory. No separate delivery or process queue is introduced by this adapter.

## Run the three original services

The services may run together against the same prepared installation.

| Role | Original source command | Readiness |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Operator | native/launch_operator.py | Exact private process record; original authenticated local browser |
| Ingress | notification_outbox.py serve | Loopback /healthz on the selected nonzero port |
| Worker | notification_outbox.py run | Existing managed process lifecycle and retained outbox status |

An operator descriptor requires a new, caller-selected private ready-file path. The descriptor is stable across review and launch; it never invents a new ready filename during preparation.

~~~json
{
  "schema": "taskerarmy.operation-request.v1",
  "operation": "commands.describe",
  "installation": "/PRIVATE/taskerarmy-installation",
  "arguments": {
    "roles": ["operator", "ingress", "worker"],
    "ready_file": "/PRIVATE/run/operator-ready.json",
    "operator_port": 0,
    "ingress_port": 8094,
    "worker_interval": 2,
    "operator_token_env": "TASKER_OPERATOR_TOKEN"
  }
}
~~~

The returned argv contains the executable as its first element. A process API such as Node spawn should use executable and argv.slice(1). The descriptor's working directory is the actual installed application.

The original operator launcher writes its private ready record before announcing readiness. Its public stdout contains the instance ID, installation ID, operation ID, PID, start time, origin, selected paths and exact operator/HTML hashes. The private ready file additionally contains the authenticated browser URL. It is a private process input to the browser observer; the operation adapter does not include the URL or session token in its JSON response. The descriptor supplies the ready-file path separately.

Verify the original child PID, installation identity, selected application/database/configuration, source hashes and loopback origin against the ready record before opening that browser. Stop and reopen the operator through the existing managed lifecycle; use a fresh ready file for the new process. Ingress has an explicit nonzero port because its original server does not announce a kernel-selected ephemeral port.

The environment references listed with each role are names and presence booleans. Install the actual values through the host's ordinary private environment or secret mechanism. A missing worker webhook remains an original route configuration failure; the adapter does not infer a connection from a product name or channel label.

## Configure and receive events

configuration.read returns the entire validated configuration, its exact byte revision and environment-reference availability. Edit that selected document and pass it with the same revision to configuration.save. The original writer validates the complete document, compares the current file revision, preserves unchanged references, and atomically replaces it.

A material routing change requires a higher route generation. The source tenant, store selection, Slack installation/channel, event-state selection and credential reference belong to that original route. Older queued notices retain their original route fingerprint.

Send actual product transitions to the original authenticated ingress or invoke events.receive with their original event IDs and job versions. The JSON adapter uses the same event validator and Outbox.record method. Job versions and SQLite delivery IDs use exact decimal strings at the JavaScript boundary. The adapter converts selected values into Python integers immediately before the original business method.

events.render returns the original Slack payload for an actionable source event. It does not transmit a message. The managed worker owns transmission, dispatch leases, channel spacing, retries and provider outcomes.

## Read and recover the existing queue

queue.status returns counts, current route failures and a selected recent-delivery window. queue.list traverses the complete original delivery table with a descending ID cursor and optional tenant, status, route and job filters. The returned counts and selected page come from one SQLite read snapshot.

jobs.history traverses every saved revision for the selected original tenant/job, including quiet and stale events, with each revision's retained deliveries. Follow next_before_version until null. queue.get returns the saved original event/message and operator recovery fields for an exact delivery ID.

Use deliveries.resolve to record an actual sent, retry or cancelled decision for a recoverable delivery. Use routes.resume after the original connection has been repaired. Both call the original Outbox methods; they do not bypass current fingerprints, expiry or newer job revisions.

Named mutations retain their exact request and result in the existing SQLite database. A completed request replays its original result before consulting later routing. Queue changes and their results commit in the same original transaction. A configuration request first retains the selected previous/target revisions, then calls the original configuration CAS writer. If the file replacement completes before its response, the same request receives that exact target revision and completes its retained result. A definitive validation or CAS refusal from the original configuration writer is also retained and replayed as the same error; an I/O interruption keeps the original prepared selection for receiving. requests.get exposes the original request record for recovery.

The adapter's request journal is an additional table in the same workspace database. It is not a second event or delivery queue.

## Adopt a complete source successor

Select the complete successor source directory and a new operation ID:

~~~sh
python3 -B native/manage.py adopt-source \
  --directory /PRIVATE/taskerarmy-installation \
  --application /SELECTED/complete-successor \
  --operation-id YOUR-RETAINED-SOURCE-CHANGE-ID
~~~

The original adoption operation materializes and verifies the full successor before selecting it. It retains the prior source and application lineage while preserving the current routing and SQLite state. Stop or reconcile any managed service that still runs a prior source edition, then start its reviewed successor through the same managed lifecycle. After adoption, inspect the installation and use its new source_identity in subsequent bound operation requests.

The JSON equivalent is installation.adopt_source. It invokes the actual currently installed native implementation and uses the same original adoption journal. If its reply is lost after source selection, the original bound request can receive that exact transition: the adapter verifies its complete target source, operation ID, original input path and retained before/after installation before letting the native receiver continue. This exception applies to that selected adoption only; other stale source bindings remain conflicts.

## Export the complete customer workspace

Select a new archive path outside the active installation:

~~~sh
python3 -B native/manage.py export \
  --directory /PRIVATE/taskerarmy-installation \
  --output /PRIVATE/delivery/taskerarmy-workspace.tar.gz \
  --operation-id YOUR-RETAINED-HANDOVER-ID
~~~

The archive carries the entire selected original source, the editable application, exact routing configuration, a native consistent SQLite backup, source manifest, installation/snapshot records and prior receiving/source lineage. Every table, including named operation requests, participates in the original database inspection. The archive manifest records every member's type, length and content hash.

Keep the original snapshot operation ID and output path if observation is interrupted. A completed archive is checked and received before a new snapshot attempt is materialized. Replaying a completed snapshot returns the same verified original archive.

Live environment values, dispatch leases held by another host and operator session URLs are not configuration data. The archive carries the original retained dispatch records and receiving lineage; the receiving implementation reconciles incomplete dispatch ownership using its existing journal.

## Independently receive and reopen

~~~sh
python3 -B native/manage.py receive \
  --archive /PRIVATE/delivery/taskerarmy-workspace.tar.gz \
  --directory /PRIVATE/received-taskerarmy \
  --python /SELECTED/python3
~~~

Receiving verifies the complete archive before selecting its independent installation. The received workspace has its own installation ID, interpreter and canonical paths; original source IDs, event/message bytes, configuration and request records remain retained. The original receiving journal makes the exact archive/directory/interpreter selection repeatable.

Requests retained in a received database keep their originating installation namespace. Read one with requests.get and its original installation_id. Start a new mutation in the received installation's own namespace, while preserving source event IDs when the intended operation is replaying an original event.

Inspect the received installation, start its own operator/worker/ingress through commands.describe, and reopen the original queue, message and job history. A later handover includes its retained lineage and independently receives through the same native operation.

## Source files and provenance

The complete reusable product includes the original worker, server, browser, guides and native lifecycle/archive code, plus this JSON adapter and installation documentation. [PROVENANCE.json](PROVENANCE.json) records the complete source identities and public primary contracts. The original operator source, event validation and channel delivery implementation remain the authoritative business behavior.

Customer configuration, live credentials, actual event data, private commissioning selections and case outputs belong to their selected private installations and handovers.

# TaskerArmy installed operation API

## Transport

Run the selected complete product's native/operations.py with Python 3.11 or later. It accepts one UTF-8 JSON request through stdin, or --request /ABSOLUTE/request.json. --request - also selects stdin. The size limit is 2,097,152 bytes. Duplicate JSON keys and non-finite JSON constants are rejected.

The request schema is taskerarmy.operation-request.v1:

~~~json
{
  "schema": "taskerarmy.operation-request.v1",
  "operation": "queue.list",
  "installation": "/PRIVATE/taskerarmy-installation",
  "arguments": {"limit": 100},
  "request_id": "OPTIONAL-RETAINED-REQUEST",
  "binding": {
    "installation_id": "SELECTED-INSTALLATION-UUID",
    "source_identity": "SELECTED-64-CHARACTER-LOWERCASE-SHA256"
  }
}
~~~

Use the actual selected UUID and source identity. The binding is optional; when supplied, each supplied field must equal the selected original installation. The schema and operation are required. arguments defaults to an empty object. Undeclared request or argument fields are rejected.

request_id is required for configuration.save, events.receive, deliveries.resolve and routes.resume. It is an identifier of at most 200 ASCII characters beginning with a letter or digit and then using letters, digits, dot, underscore, colon, slash or hyphen. Native prepare/adopt/snapshot require an operation_id either in arguments or through request_id.

A successful result exits 0:

~~~json
{
  "schema": "taskerarmy.operation-result.v1",
  "ok": true,
  "operation": "queue.list",
  "request_id": null,
  "installation": {},
  "result": {},
  "replayed": false,
  "adapter_sha256": "EXACT-ENTRYPOINT-SHA256"
}
~~~

The installation summary is:

~~~text
installation_id: UUID string
operation_id: original string
source_identity: 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters
paths: {directory, application, configuration, database} — absolute strings
python: {path: absolute string, version: [major, minor, patch]}
binding: {directory: absolute string, device: decimal string, inode: decimal string}
~~~

The result field contains the original operation result described below. Installation lifecycle results also carry the complete original native records; use the stable envelope summary for the selected identity.

Errors exit 2 and use the same result schema with ok:false, operation, request_id, adapter_sha256 and error:{code,message}. They do not echo the submitted request, an environment or a traceback. The caller retains the original request and can read its existing result before deciding how to continue.

Local paths must be absolute. Selected source, configuration, archive and installation paths and their existing ancestors cannot be symbolic links. The optional Python executable keeps the original native selector’s alias resolution: it records and verifies the actual canonical interpreter and version. Initial installation and independent receiving select a separate private directory. Snapshot output is outside the active installation.

## Exact numeric values

Queue/history delivery IDs and job versions, delivery_id and returned next cursors are decimal strings. Input delivery_id, before_id, before_version and event.version accept a positive decimal string or a JavaScript-safe JSON integer. They are converted to the original Python integer only at the business boundary. Never coerce returned IDs or cursors through JavaScript Number.

Any other returned integer outside JavaScript's safe range is also a decimal string. Configuration version remains numeric 1. A routing generation may be an exact decimal string on input; it is validated and written as the original integer. Limits, ports, TTL and the interpreter's version tuple remain ordinary bounded numeric settings.

## Installation lifecycle

| Operation | Arguments | Result and original implementation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| installation.prepare | application, configuration, directory; optional manifest_path, python, operation_id | Complete original installation record from manage.prepare; repeating the original selection sets replayed |
| installation.inspect | none; installation required | schema taskerarmy.installation-inspection.v1, installation, configuration, configuration_sha256, application_files, database, outbox |
| installation.adopt_source | application; optional manifest_path, operation_id; installation required | Complete original source-adoption result; envelope selects the resulting installation |
| installation.snapshot | output; optional operation_id; installation required | schema taskerarmy.snapshot-result.v1, snapshot, archive, attempt; original completed-output recovery/replay |
| installation.receive | archive_path, directory; optional python | Complete original receiving result including installation and its retained archive/lineage; exact selection replay |

Prepare and receive do not require a top-level installation. Their destination is arguments.directory. The public entrypoint's native implementation performs initial materialization. Installed inspect/adopt/snapshot load native/manage.py and native/archive.py from the selected installation.

database contains schema_sha256, integrity and a complete tables array. Each table record has name, columns, rows and sha256. Original SQLite tables and the named-operation journal are included. Source and archive results carry their complete file manifests and original identifiers.

## Configuration

configuration.read takes no arguments. configuration.save takes:

~~~text
revision: exact 64-character revision returned by configuration.read
configuration: complete selected configuration document
~~~

Both return:

~~~text
configuration:
  version: 1
  product_name: string
  tenants:
    tenant-id:
      ingress_token_env: environment-reference name
      review_origins: canonical HTTPS origins
  routes: array of
    id, tenant_id, store_ids, states, team_id, channel_id, webhook_env,
    generation, enabled
revision: exact SHA256 of the selected configuration bytes
credentials:
  tenants: {tenant-id: environment-reference-present boolean}
  routes: {route-id: environment-reference-present boolean}
~~~

The configuration contains names of environment variables, not their values. The returned booleans report the reference availability observed by that operation. A completed named replay retains its original result; configuration.read obtains the current host's availability. Save the complete document you opened. Unchanged references stay unchanged; the original CAS and route-generation rules govern concurrent updates.

For a named configuration request, the same SQLite database retains the exact request and its intended previous/target revisions before the original configuration writer runs. A repeated completed request returns its retained result. A repeated prepared request continues only from its retained previous or target file revision. configuration_outcome_changed identifies a current file that matches neither selection.

## Queue status and complete listing

queue.status arguments are optional tenant and limit (1–1000, default100). It returns the original:

~~~text
counts: [{status, count}]
deliveries: recent original delivery summaries, descending by ID
route_failures: [{route_id, reason, failed_at}]
~~~

queue.list arguments:

~~~text
tenant?: original tenant ID
status?: original saved status
route_id?: original route ID
job_id?: original job ID
before_id?: exclusive descending delivery-ID cursor
limit?: integer1–1000, default100
~~~

Result:

~~~text
deliveries: [{
  id, tenant_id, route_id, event_id, job_id, version,
  channel_key, message_sha256, status, attempts,
  due_at, expires_at, created_at, updated_at,
  http_status, last_error, sent_at, resolution
}]
counts: [{status, count}] — complete matching collection, before the page cursor
total: sum of the matching counts
next_before_id: exact decimal string, or null
filters: the selected tenant/status/route_id/job_id values
~~~

All filters combine. Counts and the selected page are read in one original SQLite transaction. Continue with the same filters and returned next_before_id until it is null. A new page is a new database snapshot: concurrent worker transitions remain current, while the cursor follows stable original row IDs.

queue.get takes delivery_id and returns the original operator's safe projection of the saved delivery. It includes the saved event, exact Slack message, message hash, resolution and can_resolve flag. Private dispatch lease tokens are excluded.

## Complete job history

jobs.history takes tenant, job, optional before_version, and limit (1–1000, default100).

~~~text
job: {
  tenant_id, job_id, store_id, version, event_id, state, updated_at
} or null
events: [{
  event_id, version, state, received_at, outcome, payload_hash,
  deliveries: [{
    id, route_id, channel_key, status, attempts, http_status,
    last_error, sent_at, resolution, message_sha256
  }]
}]
next_before_version: exclusive descending decimal-string cursor, or null
~~~

The original job head is returned with every page. Each page preserves recorded revisions including quiet and stale outcomes. Continue the same original tenant/job and next_before_version through the full history.

## Original event and recovery operations

| Operation | Arguments | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| events.receive | tenant, event, optional ttl_seconds | Original Outbox.record result: outcome, queued and original_outcome for an original duplicate |
| events.render | tenant, event | Original Slack Block Kit payload for an actionable event |
| deliveries.resolve | delivery_id, outcome, note | delivery_id and resulting status |
| routes.resume | route_id | route_id and resumed original delivery count |

events.receive defaults ttl_seconds to86400 and accepts60–604800. The source event includes event_id, job_id, store_id, version, state, occurred_at, title, review_url and optional reason. The original worker validates the exact tenant/review-origin contract and event fields. The state vocabulary and source publisher hook are documented in the application guide.

Rendering does not save or transmit. Receiving saves through the original Outbox method. The managed original worker performs delivery.

A resolution outcome is sent, retry or cancelled. note is the operator's original resolution explanation. The original delivery must be in a recoverable state; retry keeps its original route identity. Resume requires a corrected and enabled original route.

Each named queue mutation calls the unchanged original method inside one original SQLite transaction and commits its request result with the business change. The adapter does not implement a parallel event or delivery state machine.

## Read a retained request

requests.get takes request_id and optional installation_id. The default namespace is the selected installation. The result is {request:null} when absent, or:

~~~text
request:
  installation_id, request_id, operation, request_sha256,
  request_json: exact canonical original UTF-8 request as a string
  request: decoded original request
  state: prepared or completed
  result: retained preparation or completed operation result
  created_at, completed_at, source_identity, adapter_sha256
~~~

A completed result may contain a definitive original configuration validation/CAS refusal with schema taskerarmy.operation-rejection.v1, error:{code,message}, previous_revision and target_revision. Replaying that named operation returns the same original error. Filesystem or transport uncertainty remains prepared so the exact target can still be received after an interrupted replacement.

The journal remains in the original database and survives full snapshot/receiving. A received installation has a new namespace; supply the originating installation_id to inspect that original request. Completed responses are received before later routing or configuration validation. The exact original request_json remains available for a byte-consistent replay through stdin.

## Managed command descriptions

commands.describe takes:

~~~text
roles?: distinct selection of operator, ingress, worker; defaults to all three
ready_file: required absolute private output path when operator is selected
operator_port?: 0–65535, default0
ingress_port?: 1–65535, default8094
worker_interval?: 0.1–60 seconds, default2
operator_token_env?: supported environment-reference name, default TASKER_OPERATOR_TOKEN
~~~

It returns {commands,installation}. Each command contains:

~~~text
role: operator | ingress | worker
executable: actual absolute selected Python executable
argv: complete array including that executable as argv[0]
cwd: actual installed application
script: absolute original Python source entrypoint
script_sha256: exact selected source-file SHA256
ready_file: selected private path for operator, otherwise null
health: readiness descriptor
environment_references: [{name, present}]
~~~

Original command forms:

~~~text
operator:
  PYTHON -B APP/native/launch_operator.py --directory INSTALL
  --ready-file PRIVATE_FILE --port PORT --token-env ENV_NAME

ingress:
  PYTHON -B APP/notification_outbox.py --db DB --config CONFIG
  serve --host 127.0.0.1 --port PORT

worker:
  PYTHON -B APP/notification_outbox.py --db DB --config CONFIG
  run --interval SECONDS
~~~

The operator health descriptor is {kind:"private-ready-file",path,schema:"taskerarmy.operator-process.v1"}. Ingress is {kind:"http",url:"http://127.0.0.1:PORT/healthz"}. Worker is {kind:"managed-process"}.

The original operator ready record has schema, instance_id, installation_id, operation_id, pid, started_at, origin, application, database, configuration, operator_source_sha256 and html_sha256. The private file additionally has the authenticated browser URL. Stdout announces every listed identity field and omits that URL. Neither the descriptor nor the operation result includes session tokens, webhook values or environment contents.

An existing managed supervisor owns the child and its inherited process lease. It should select one resource key per installation/role, verify exact source and child identity, consume the private operator URL in its browser observer, and close or restart the same managed service through its original lifecycle.

## Local error handling and replay

Preserve a mutation's request ID, full arguments and selected binding before dispatch. A matching completed request returns the retained result with replayed:true. Reusing the ID for another operation or request body returns request_conflict. A changed supplied installation binding returns installation_changed. Source adoption has one narrow continuation: the original prior source binding can receive that exact already-selected adoption when its operation ID, complete target source/manifest, original input path, retained prior request and full selected before/after transition all match. Its original native adoption receiver handles the completed result or a selected-pointer/result-write interruption. A different input, operation, installation or later source edition remains a binding conflict.

The adapter reports original validation and local source/database errors in one JSON result. Read requests.get after an uncertain response. The original snapshot and receiving journals own archive replay; their identities remain in the returned native records. Configuration CAS and uncertain Slack transmission require their original reconciliation paths, as described in the application and operator guides.

const read = {readOnly: true, idempotent: true};
const selected = {workspace};
const named = {workspace, requestId: uuid};
const page = {limit: {type: 'integer', minimum: 1, maximum: 200}};
const event = {type: 'object', description: 'Complete original Tasker event. Preserve a large version as a decimal string.'};
export function taskerWorkspaceTools(tool) {
  return [
    tool('merchant_tasker_status', 'Inspect the original Tasker installation, source identity, database path and selected Python.',
      selected, ['workspace'], read),
    tool('merchant_tasker_prepare', 'Prepare the complete original Tasker application at the host-selected private directory and configuration. Retain the request UUID across interruption.',
      named, ['workspace', 'requestId'], {idempotent: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_adopt_source', 'Adopt the complete host-selected original source edition in the same installation. Review its current identity first; keep the request UUID.',
      named, ['workspace', 'requestId'], {idempotent: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_snapshot', 'Export the complete original application, configuration and SQLite database to the configured transfer directory, using this UUID as the archive filename.',
      named, ['workspace', 'requestId'], {idempotent: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_receive', 'Independently receive the complete host-selected original archive into this alias’s selected directory.',
      named, ['workspace', 'requestId'], {idempotent: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_configuration', 'Read the whole original configuration and its current revision. Credentials are environment-reference names and presence booleans.',
      selected, ['workspace'], read),
    tool('merchant_tasker_save_configuration', 'Save the whole original configuration at its exact current revision. Retain the request UUID; an exact retry recovers its committed result.',
      {...named, revision: digest, configuration: {type: 'object'}},
      ['workspace', 'requestId', 'revision', 'configuration'], {idempotent: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_queue_status', 'Read the original queue summary, route circuits and recent deliveries.',
      {...selected, tenant: identifier, ...page}, ['workspace'], read),
    tool('merchant_tasker_queue', 'Page the original deliveries with complete filtered counts. Keep filters and follow next_before_id; delivery IDs are exact decimal strings.',
      {...selected, tenant: identifier, status: identifier, routeId: identifier, jobId: identifier, beforeId: decimal, ...page},
      ['workspace'], read),
    tool('merchant_tasker_delivery', 'Read one complete original delivery before resolving an uncertain send.',
      {...selected, deliveryId: decimal}, ['workspace', 'deliveryId'], read),
    tool('merchant_tasker_job_history', 'Read the original job’s retained event versions with exact decimal version cursors.',
      {...selected, tenant: identifier, jobId: identifier, beforeVersion: decimal, ...page},

    tool('merchant_tasker_receive_event', 'Validate and enqueue the complete original event under its tenant and source version rules. This does not execute a Slack send; the original worker handles eligible deliveries.',

      ['workspace', 'requestId', 'tenant', 'event'], {idempotent: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_render_event', 'Render the same original event and selected routes without enqueuing it.',
      {...selected, tenant: identifier, event}, ['workspace', 'tenant', 'event'], read),
    tool('merchant_tasker_resolve_delivery', 'Resolve the selected original uncertain delivery with its real sent, retry or cancelled outcome and operator note.',
      {...named, deliveryId: decimal, outcome: {type: 'string', enum: ['sent', 'retry', 'cancelled']},
        note: {type: 'string', minLength: 1, maxLength: 300}},
      ['workspace', 'requestId', 'deliveryId', 'outcome', 'note'], {idempotent: true, destructive: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_resume_route', 'Resume the original paused route after reviewing its circuit and delivery state.',
      {...named, routeId: identifier}, ['workspace', 'requestId', 'routeId'], {idempotent: true}),
    tool('merchant_tasker_request', 'Recover a named operation from the same original SQLite database after an interrupted reply.',
      {...selected, requestId: nativeRequest, originInstallationId: uuid}, ['workspace', 'requestId'], read),

# Tasker notification installations in Stellar Forge

The installed product includes the original Python notification outbox, tenant-routed event receiver, browser operator, complete application and SQLite archive, and independent receiving workflow. The SCF integration adds a typed local client, source-owned MCP provider, CLI and three Applications entries around that same installation.

Python 3.11 or later runs the native product. The JavaScript integration uses the installed Stellar Forge Node runtime and Node built-ins. The standalone Python application needs no additional packages.

## Prepare the complete original application

Keep the application source, installation directory and transfer directory separate. Select an owned private parent and a complete configuration file. The included configuration.empty.json is a useful starting document; configure the actual tenants, review origins and routes in the operator. It contains environment-reference names and no credential values.

Run the distributed taskerarmy command through the existing forge command runner, or run its complete CLI directly:

~~~sh
node products/taskerarmy/cli.mjs prepare \
  --application /ABSOLUTE/SELECTED_SOURCE/products/taskerarmy \
  --configuration /PRIVATE/notices.json \
  --directory /PRIVATE/tasker-installation \
  --python /ABSOLUTE/python3 \
  --request-id 3d9e3935-7c02-4fd5-86d3-2b719571a9c0

node products/taskerarmy/cli.mjs inspect \
  --directory /PRIVATE/tasker-installation \
  --python /ABSOLUTE/python3
~~~

Use the actual absolute Python executable and a newly selected UUID for your operation. Keep that UUID and complete source/configuration selection when continuing the same request. Preparation retains both the original source and editable application, the complete source manifest, selected interpreter, tenant configuration and SQLite database.

The native application and its public operation adapter are documented in README.md, OPERATOR.md, native/README.md and native/API.md. Those guides describe the actual event states, publisher mapping, route-generation rules, retry policy and uncertain-send recovery.

## Open the three original services in Applications

Select the current installed Stellar Forge runtime containing the Tasker distribution contribution. Add these entries against the same prepared installation:

| Entry | Purpose | Selection |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Tasker notification operator | Edit the original tenant/route configuration and inspect events and delivery recovery | Prepared private directory, Python, loopback operator port; 0 chooses an available port |
| Tasker event receiver | Accept authenticated source events into the original database | The same directory and environment; blank or 0 selects fixed port 8094 |
| Tasker delivery worker | Dispatch the original eligible queue and recover its retries/circuits | The same directory and environment; interval defaults to 2 seconds |

Use a different fixed ingress port for each installation. Its original GET /healthz reports readiness. Operator and ingress listen on loopback.

Select the required credential references through Applications' existing private environment JSON. Each tenant's ingress token and each enabled route's Slack webhook are supplied only to the original service environment. The operator generates a private session token unless TASKER_OPERATOR_TOKEN is selected.

Review, Save and Start retain the actual installation UUID, original source identity, current application inventory, configuration revision and Python selection. Each installation/role has one Applications resource identity, allowing all three roles to coexist. The existing managed worker launches the original Python process directly and passes its held worker lease through descriptor 3.

Each actual operator launch receives a fresh private ready-file path inside that same managed operation. Its exact argv is retained in the existing command-process record. The startup observer checks the actual child PID, complete private/public identity, selected installation paths and original Python/HTML hashes. Applications receives the authenticated browser URL through its existing private URL record. The public process announcement contains the origin and original identity.

Stop and restart each role through its saved Applications entry. The original database and source history remain in that installation. A changed source or configuration is reviewed through the current saved selection.

## Use the host-selected MCP workspace

Create a private JSON connection file, for example:

~~~json
{
  "schema": "stellar-forge.tasker-workspace-connection.v1",
  "workspaces": {
    "operations": {
      "label": "Notification operations",
      "directory": "/PRIVATE/tasker-installation",
      "sourceDirectory": "/ABSOLUTE/SELECTED_SOURCE/products/taskerarmy",
      "application": "/ABSOLUTE/SELECTED_SOURCE/products/taskerarmy",
      "python": "/ABSOLUTE/python3",
      "configurationFile": "/PRIVATE/notices.json",
      "transferDirectory": "/PRIVATE/transfers"
    }
  }
}
~~~

Set the actual absolute paths. The connection file must be owned and private (0600), with canonical source and installation paths. A new installation path is permitted below its existing private parent. transferDirectory must already be private. A receiving alias can select receiveArchive and its separate new destination. Optional binding selects an original installation_id and source_identity.

The distribution declares merchant provider tasker-workspaces, family/configuration key taskerWorkspaces, and the host configuration input taskerWorkspaceConnection. The original merchant registry discovers its metadata and loads its native implementation when configured. Its configuration reader is readTaskerWorkspaceConfiguration.

For direct use of the same configured provider:

~~~js
import {readTaskerWorkspaceConfiguration, MerchantTaskerWorkspaces}
  from './products/taskerarmy/workspace.mjs';

const taskerWorkspaces = await readTaskerWorkspaceConfiguration('/PRIVATE/tasker-connection.json');
const owner = new MerchantTaskerWorkspaces({taskerWorkspaces});
try {
  const selected = await owner.call('merchant_tasker_status', {workspace: 'operations'});
  const page = await owner.call('merchant_tasker_queue', {workspace: 'operations', limit: 100});
  console.log(selected.installation, page.result);
} finally {
  await owner.close();
}
~~~

Closing this adapter drains its pending native calls. Applications continues to own its running services.

### Complete operation surface

| MCP tools | Original operation |
| --- | --- |
| merchant_tasker_status / prepare / adopt_source | Inspect or prepare the original complete installation and adopt a selected source edition |
| merchant_tasker_snapshot / receive | Export complete original application and SQLite state, then independently receive that archive |
| merchant_tasker_configuration / save_configuration | Read the complete environment-reference configuration and save it at its exact revision |
| merchant_tasker_queue_status / queue / delivery | Read the original summary, fully paginated filtered queue and complete selected delivery |
| merchant_tasker_job_history | Follow the original tenant/job's complete version history |
| merchant_tasker_receive_event / render_event | Save or render the exact validated publisher event |
| merchant_tasker_resolve_delivery / resume_route | Apply the original operator's actual delivery decision and corrected-route recovery |
| merchant_tasker_request | Read a retained original request; select originInstallationId for a journal copied from another installation |
| merchant_tasker_commands | Describe the actual original native service argv and credential-reference presence |

Mutations use a retained UUID in the host adapter. The original operation API also accepts its documented plain request identifiers. Queue/history delivery IDs, event versions and cursors travel as exact decimal strings. A JavaScript caller must not convert those returned values to Number. Follow next_before_id and next_before_version with the same filters until null.

The queue change and named request result commit in the original SQLite transaction. Configuration saving uses the original configuration revision and writer, with the named request retaining its selected previous and target file revisions. After an interrupted result, inspect that same original request before deciding how to continue.

## Full local client and CLI

The typed TaskerInstallation client exposes every native operation, including install/receive/snapshot, configuration, queue/history, events, delivery recovery and named requests. client.d.mts retains the installation and exact-decimal result shapes.

~~~js
import {TaskerInstallation} from './products/taskerarmy/client.mjs';
const client = new TaskerInstallation({
  directory: '/PRIVATE/tasker-installation',
  sourceDirectory: '/ABSOLUTE/SELECTED_SOURCE/products/taskerarmy',
  python: '/ABSOLUTE/python3'
});
try {
  const configuration = await client.configuration();
  const page = await client.queue({limit: 100});
  console.log(configuration.result.revision, page.result.next_before_id);
} finally {
  await client.close();
}
~~~

For an exact native operation from the CLI, save its arguments as one private JSON object and use:

~~~sh
node products/taskerarmy/cli.mjs call \
  --directory /PRIVATE/tasker-installation \
  --operation jobs.history \
  --arguments /PRIVATE/history-arguments.json
~~~

history-arguments.json contains the complete selected tenant, job and optional before_version/limit. A mutation additionally uses --request-id. The CLI also exposes the original services directly; the operator requires a fresh --ready-file, ingress defaults to fixed port8094, and the worker interval defaults to2. Applications provides the shared supervision and retained launch selection.

## Complete receiving and onward export

The native archive format is TAR.GZ. It carries the complete selected original and editable application sources, configuration, original SQLite backup, manifest, snapshots, lineage and native operation journal.

~~~sh
node products/taskerarmy/cli.mjs snapshot \
  --directory /PRIVATE/tasker-installation \
  --output /PRIVATE/transfers/tasker-complete.tar.gz \
  --request-id 27e1da41-8b44-4dc2-b175-86f8ebef51d6

node products/taskerarmy/cli.mjs receive \
  --directory /PRIVATE/tasker-received \
  --archive /PRIVATE/transfers/tasker-complete.tar.gz \
  --python /ABSOLUTE/python3 \
  --request-id 95d2cc18-f615-4f1e-bce3-c73f025e4f67
~~~

Keep the complete original archive and its returned byte count, digest and native manifest. Receiving creates a new installation identity while preserving the original lineage and database. Inspect the copied operation journal with the originating installation UUID, then open the received operator, inspect the actual queue/history and export the received installation onward. The native receiving request and completed outputs govern retries.
